questions.problem: Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=3{e}^{2\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi .$
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3{e}^{2\theta }$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{(3{e}^{2\theta })}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}{e}^{4\theta }\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{9}{8}({e}^{4\pi }-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{9}{8}({e}^{4\pi }-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(4-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi })) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{8}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\pi -0)+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{4}+2(-2)-\frac{1}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{9\pi -16}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi .$
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(4-8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(-1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-2(-\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi })) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }) \\  & =3\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =3(\pi -\frac{\pi }{2})+4(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}+4\cdot (-1)-\frac{1}{2}(0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}-4 \\  & =\frac{3\pi -8}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

When $r(\theta )=2{e}^{\theta }$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}(2{e}^{\theta })^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}4{e}^{2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2}){|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)} \\  & ={e}^{2\theta }\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}-{e}^{0} \\  & =4-1 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$
